content: The process of improving the collection and use of administrative data on violence against women (VAW) involves several critical steps and considerations. In Uganda, for example, mapping the administrative data environment and harmonizing data collection practices are essential to creating a functional VAW administrative data system. This system must assess the willingness and capacity of relevant data producers to participate. Depending on feasibility, the system may initially focus on specialized VAW service providers or expand to include general service providers across sectors. Specialized VAW services, such as family and domestic violence units within police or justice systems, have trained personnel with a clear mandate to address VAW. This focus simplifies implementation but risks excluding survivors who do not access these specialized services. For instance, many survivors report violence to general police officers or seek healthcare from non-specialized services, such as emergency departments or obstetrics and gynecology units. While general services can capture data from a broader range of survivors, the quality of data may suffer without adequate training and resources. A phased approach to data collection, starting with specialized services and expanding to general services, may be necessary. Training general service providers to understand and respond to VAW, including data collection, represents an opportunity to improve services for survivors. Even if initial data collection is limited, it can raise awareness of VAW within general services and lead to long-term improvements in data quality and service delivery. Administrative data on VAW should ideally be collected from both specialized and general services. This requires coordination among stakeholders, including policymakers, service managers, academics, civil society organizations, and international partners. Regular dialogue between data producers and users can strengthen trust, improve data quality, and align data collection with user needs. For example, in Jamaica, multi-sectoral dialogues were held to identify data needs and gaps, leading to the development of a minimum data set for VAW administrative data. The minimum data set should include variables such as the number, age, and gender of survivors and perpetrators, the survivor-perpetrator relationship, types of violence experienced (e.g., physical, sexual, psychological, financial), and services provided to survivors. Collecting this data allows sectors to monitor service demand, describe key characteristics of survivors and perpetrators, and understand the types of violence for which services are sought. Additional variables, such as location of violence, gender identity, and disability status, may also be included based on national priorities. Data collection must be survivor-centered, ensuring confidentiality and avoiding harm. Feedback mechanisms, such as anonymous complaints systems or independent research on survivors’ experiences, can complement administrative data. Engaging civil society organizations and survivors in the design and governance of data systems is crucial to ensuring their effectiveness and ethical integrity. Standardized operational definitions and response options for variables across sectors are essential for harmonizing data collection. For example, behavioral definitions of VAW, based on acts committed by perpetrators, allow for consistent data categories across settings. Even in the absence of specific laws criminalizing certain forms of VAW, such as marital rape, recording the survivor-perpetrator relationship can make these forms of violence visible and contribute to the realization of international human rights standards. Finally, metadata should be created to document the context of data production, including the time period and stage of reporting. Tools and guidelines are available to support the development of metadata and the alignment of administrative data with statistical classifications. By addressing these considerations, countries can build comprehensive and effective systems for collecting and using administrative data on VAW, ultimately improving prevention and response efforts.
